newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX rebounds, sets aside Friday's jitters.
newsitem.headline: German DAX rebounds, sets aside Friday's jitters.

text.p: German shares got the week off to a bullish start on Monday, eliminating more than half of Friday's dramatic losses in early dealings amid relief at a relatively minor fall on Wall Street and a firmer dollar.
The 30-share DAX index was up 71.27 points, or 2.55 percent, at 2,863.23 points at 0939 GMT, making up much of its four percent tumble on Friday.
"I am totally bullish. The market has had the weekend to digest what happened last week and is in far calmer form," said one Munich dealer.
"I think we can still see the 2,900-point level (on the DAX) by the end of the year," he added.
Dealers said the market was re-evaluating the comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan last week about excessive market gains which triggered a global rout on stocks.
"People are starting to see that the first reaction was a bit too exaggerated," said one Frankfurt dealer.
"In Germany, at least, most of the sales on Friday were driven by traders themselves," the Munich dealer said.
"The real money, the institutional investors, did not want to play along, which is what makes me optimistic," he added.
A firm start by Bunds and the dollar's return to trade over 1.55 marks were also helping to buoy stocks.
Gains were spread across the board, with little major corporate news about. Chemical shares, Friday's biggest losers, were among the top gainers.

Utility Viag AG was up 12.5 marks at 595 marks after its packaging manufacturing unit Schmalbach Lubeca announced plans for a U.S. acquisition. Dealers said the news was mildly positive, indicating Viag's willingness to concentrate on core business areas.

Insurer Allianz AG Holding was up 57 marks at 2,842 marks, as rumours buzzed about its reported plans to sell a 15 percent stake in BHF Bank. The group has denied it has concrete plans to do so but has not ruled out the prospect completely.
"Something is going to happen there, we are sure of that," said a Frankfurt trader.
